name: Fuscous
lede: Fuscous is a dark, dull, greenish-brown grey, from a Latin root for brown and dusky, kept alive in Ridgway's color nomenclature.

sections.title: A dusky word
sections.body: The Latin root *fusc-* means brown, tawny or dark, and Paterson's dictionary defines fuscous as brown, dingy, dark or sombre, and also as a brownish grey [1]. The same root gives *fuscescent* (dark brownish) and *fusco-ferruginous* (rust-colored) [1]. It was a descriptive word before it was a swatch, and Paterson's lists place it among the browns [2].

sections.title: Ridgway's swatch
sections.body: Our library traces the color to Ridgway's plate XLVI of 1912, and the ISCC-NBS system files the nearest block as olive gray, only 2.2 units away on the CIEDE2000 scale [3]. That is a very close fit, so the swatch here is near the standard one [3]. It is a warm dark neutral that sits between [[olive-grey]] and [[brown-grey]] [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color this close appears in 2,887 works, or 12.1 per cent, which makes it more common than 94 per cent of the named colors [4]. Aged varnish dulls and darkens colors, so some of these matches may once have been browns or greens [4]. The 1100s show a peak, but there are only 50 paintings from that century in the archive, so that figure is weak [4]. Read all of this as screen color, not pigment evidence [4].

origin.source: Paterson, A Dictionary of Colour; Ridgway 1912
